Final Technical Report 15/57 3.2 Environmental Conditions Defining an environmental envelope against which the MTV will be designed is crucial for the vessel’s survivability and lifecycle. The MTV is expected to operate in three different settings: ocean currents, tides, and river/estuaries, for which environmental conditions can vary widely. The aim is to create an envelope that ensures the platform's flexibility in a wide range of weather conditions. Therefore, an exhaustive analysis of some of the most optimal and demanding locations for current energy harvesting across the US was carried out during the preliminary design phase. In this section, a brief summary of the observed conditions is provided. 3.2.1 Ocean current location - Florida Ocean currents are defined as the continuous, predictable, directional movement of seawater driven by gravity, wind, and water density. Various sites where the ocean currents could be accessed in the U.S. have been analyzed, and it has been determined that the area with the fastest current speeds is an area offshore the southeast coast of Florida. At the fastest sites, these current velocities usually range between 1 and 3 m/s. Florida, in particular, was of high interest due to the Gulf Stream passing by its coast. This section, called the Florida Current, and its northern extension, the North Atlantic Drift, is a warm and swift Atlantic Ocean current that originates in the Gulf of Mexico and flows through the Straits of Florida. These currents travel up the eastern coastline of the United States, then veer east near 36° North latitude (North Carolina), and then toward Northwest Europe as the North Atlantic Current. Following FAU's advice, one particular location has been chosen for MTV use. The location proposed by FAU is north of Boca Raton, Florida, and south of West Palm Beach, Florida, at coordinates 26°28'12.00"N and 79°53'24.00"W. This location is representative of the conditions found off the coast of southeast Florida, where the Gulf Stream is closest to the U.S., and the depths are hundreds of meters (290 m at the proposed location). As a result, this depth requires the use of an external mooring system, and due to the unidirectionality of ocean currents, a single-point mooring is likely suitable.
